extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy and aesthetics (scholars of art, architecture, and mental philosophy)
extracted.subtask_short: aesthetic evaluation of art and architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative principles for natural beauty, fine art, and architectural aesthetics as set out in a philosophical treatise; includes related standards about mental health/madness relevant to testimony and recollection. Useful for critiquing or producing works in art, landscape design, architecture, and for assessing coherence of memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and consistency of nature in landscape beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The sight of a beautiful landscape delights because of the perfect truth and consistency of nature: every modification (position, foreshortening, concealment, distance, lighting, perspective) is unerringly given and accurately taken account of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate landscapes for visual coherence and accurate relations of forms and lighting; the more consistent and 'scrupulously right' the visible connections, the stronger the æsthetic effect. Anti-pattern: scenes with obvious visual contradictions or inconsistent perspective reduce the aesthetic delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purifying, corrective effect of a beautiful view
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful view sets the brain in perfectly normal action and disposes formal thought to greater correctness; it acts as a cathartic of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works for their capacity to harmonize and 'purify' thought—i.e., whether engagement with the work leads to clearer, more orderly thinking. This is an effect-based criterion rather than mere formal property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence and the sublime (mountain line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that suggest permanence (e.g., mountain chains that defy decay) contribute to a serious or sublime mood because they contrast with human ephemerality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating sublimity, consider elements that convey endurance and immutability; the emotional tone may be partly explained by such formal cues even if not consciously articulated by the beholder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate lighting for subject (human vs landscape)
rubrics_metrics.description: Light from above is most advantageous for the human form and countenance, whereas for landscape the converse often holds true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider direction of light as a formal criterion: the same lighting that flatters portraiture may be unfavourable for landscape composition. Use lighting deliberately according to subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent naturalness / concealment of artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Spots left free to nature (absent the hand of man) immediately decorate themselves in a tasteful manner; gardens are most beautiful when art is concealed so nature appears to move freely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design or judge landscapes and gardens by the degree to which artifice is hidden and nature's spontaneity appears; anti-pattern: overt, mechanical ornamentation that proclaims the possessor's will (e.g., clipped hedges, forced shapes) diminishes beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of expression (objectivity vs subjectivity in gardens)
rubrics_metrics.description: English/Chinese gardens are planned in an objective spirit expressing nature's Ideas, whereas French gardens mirror the possessor's will; the former is more æsthetically correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate landscape design for whether it expresses 'the will of nature' (authentic, organic forms) rather than merely reflecting the owner's subjective imposition. Example: clipped, geometrical French parterres are subjective impositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art aims to show life/truth perceptually, not conceptually
rubrics_metrics.description: Every genuine work of art answers 'What is life?' through the naive language of perception (images, sensory presentation), not through abstract, reflective conceptualising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works by how well they convey life's nature via perceptible images that invite the beholder's perception and fancy; artworks that reduce their aim to explicit conceptual statements are viewed as inferior or ungenuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for co-operation of the beholder (interpretive participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of art produces its effect only through the fancy of the beholder; the spectator must contribute from his own capacity and culture to bring the work's wisdom to light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work invites and rewards active interpretive engagement. Anti-pattern: works that force-feed all meanings to the viewer, leaving no space for imagination or personal response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave something for the imagination (incompleteness as a virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: A work of art should not give everything to the senses; it must supply only so much as leads the fancy on, leaving the ultimate thing for the imagination to complete—'Le secret d'être ennuyeux, c'est de tout dire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate completeness vs suggestiveness: greater æsthetic value when essential elements are suggested rather than exhaustively specified. Example anti-pattern: wax figures fail as fine art because they present form and colour fully, excluding the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid communicating art's kernel as a mere distinct conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Works of art arising from mere distinct conceptions (i.e., fully thinkable/expressible beforehand) are ungenuine because the conception is exhaustible and should not be the medium of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge authenticity by origin: if the artist could beforehand state in precise words what the work intends to present, the work may be a mere illustration of a concept and thus artistically deficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper relation of means to ends (no arbitrary playing)
rubrics_metrics.description: An arbitrary playing with the means of art without knowledge of the end identifies the dabbler; such works exhibit aimless ornament, senseless runs, jingling rhymes, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate technical choices for purposefulness: do formal devices serve the work's deeper aim, or are they gratuitous? Anti-pattern: decorative elements that support nothing or musical/poetic 'jingling' without substantive end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of inspiration and immediacy vs limitations of large works
rubrics_metrics.description: Works produced in an ecstatic inspiration (sketches, lyrical songs, melodies) are purely delightful and inevitable; great long works (epics, operas, grand paintings) require reflection and craft and thus often include insipid or wearisome parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating large-scale works, allow for admixture of technical filler necessary to connect inspired parts; but also recognise the special value of immediacy in small, inspired pieces. Expects some compromise in extended compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts communicate Ideas perceptibly; philosophy communicates them conceptually
rubrics_metrics.description: Art communicates the Ideas of the world 'virtualiter' (implicitly) through perception and is inexhaustible; philosophy aims to make the same truth explicit and determinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat art's success as measured by its capacity to make Ideas perceptible and inexhaustible; art that attempts to function like philosophy (exhaustively stating its idea) fails aesthetically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture's fundamental theme: support and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: The one constant theme of pure æsthetics of architecture is support and burden; fundamental law: no burden without sufficient support and no support without a suitable burden—the relation must fit exactly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate buildings for honesty and appropriateness of structural expression: elements should visibly correspond to their structural role. Example of ideal: column and entablature where support and burden are completely separated. Anti-pattern: forms that suggest support when none exists, or conceal structural truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of support and burden as aesthetic principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic effect increases with the separation of support and burden (colonnade being pure separation); fused support/burden (plain wall, vaulting where each stone is both) yields less pure æsthetic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess degree of separation: colonnade > vault/pier > plain wall in terms of clarity of the structural theme. Consider the visual legibility of load-bearing relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural appropriateness (use of columns, pilasters, vaults)
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural devices (columns, pilasters, consoles, vaults) realize the separation or fusion of support and burden; where necessary, even representations (painted pilasters) can indicate an order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether architectural elements are used to express or merely imitate structural truths; use of faux devices may be acceptable to indicate order, but the æsthetic ideal is genuine realization of support/burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of perfect recollection as health of mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The health of the mind properly consists in perfect recollection: while not everything is retained, peculiar or significant events must be findable in memory; madness is described as a broken thread of memory and incoherent recollection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this as a diagnostic/evaluative standard for mental soundness: certainty about past witnessed events and continuity of recollection marks sanity; frequent doubts about reality of remembered events, or self-deception through repeated fabrication, indicate insanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of madness: will resisting intellect / suppression of adverse facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Madness may arise when the will resists allowing certain injurious or adverse facts to be assimilated by the intellect, producing suppression and gaps that are filled arbitrarily, leading to delusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the psychological dynamic in assessing causes of delusion: look for evidence that painful facts were actively repressed and replaced by fabrications. This is an explanatory criterion rather than a prescriptive one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frenzy (mania sine delirio) as withdrawal of will from reflective reason
rubrics_metrics.description: A state of frenzy occurs when the will periodically withdraws from the government of the intellect: reflective knowledge is suspended while intuitive consciousness remains, producing violent, destructive action without reflective guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between lack of reflection (frenzy) and loss of intuition; in frenzy the subject still apprehends objects and later remembers actions, but acts without reflection. Use this to classify presentations of violent, unreflective behaviour.
